text: Welcome the one who is weak in faith, but not for the sake of quarreling over opinions.
One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables.
The one who eats must not look down on the one who does not, and the one who does not eat must not pass judgment on the one who does, for God has welcomed him.
Who are you to judge someone else's servant? He stands or falls before his own master—and he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand.
One person regards one day above another; another regards every day alike. Let each be fully convinced in his own mind.
Whoever observes the day observes it to the Lord. Whoever eats does so to the Lord, since he gives thanks to God; and whoever abstains does so to the Lord, and he too gives thanks to God.
For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself.
If we live, we live to the Lord; and if we die, we die to the Lord. So whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord.
For this is why Christ died and returned to life: that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living.
But you—why do you judge your brother? And you—why do you look down on your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God.

versions.text: Why, then, do you judge your brother? Or why do you look down on your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God.
versions.explanation: The emphatic pronoun σύ in both questions marks a pointed turn to the individual reader; rendering it gives the rhetorical punch and rhythm of the Greek, which the flat "Why, then" loses.

text: As it is written: "As I live, says the Lord, every knee will bow to me, and every tongue will confess to God."
So then, each of us will give an account of himself.

versions.text: So then, each of us will give an account of himself to God.
versions.explanation: The base text here does not include "to God" (τῷ θεῷ); it appears only in part of the manuscript tradition. Either drop the phrase or retain it with a footnote noting that some manuscripts add "to God."

text: Therefore let us stop judging one another. Instead, resolve never to put a stumbling block or obstacle in your brother's way.
I know, and I am convinced in the Lord Jesus, that nothing is unclean in itself; but if anyone regards something as unclean, then for him it is unclean.
If your brother is distressed because of what you eat, you are no longer walking in love. Do not let your food destroy someone for whom Christ died.
So then, do not let the good that is yours be spoken of as evil.

versions.text: So do not let what is good to you be spoken of as evil.
versions.explanation: "what is good to you" is awkward and slightly misleading; the Greek has the possessive ὑμῶν modifying τὸ ἀγαθόν ("your good"), i.e., the good thing you possess or enjoy. The revised wording reads more naturally aloud and reflects the plural "your."

text: For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.
Anyone who serves Christ in this way is pleasing to God and approved by people.

versions.text: Anyone who serves Christ in this way is pleasing to God and approved by others.
versions.explanation: τοῖς ἀνθρώποις is general ("people, human beings"), not "others" in the sense of fellow believers just mentioned; "approved by people" keeps the God/people contrast clear.

text: So then, let us pursue what makes for peace and for building one another up.
Do not tear down the work of God for the sake of food. Everything is clean, but it is wrong for a person to eat in a way that causes someone else to stumble.
It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that makes your brother stumble.
The faith you have, keep between yourself and God. Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself by what he approves.
But whoever has doubts is condemned if he eats, because his eating is not from faith; and everything that is not from faith is sin.
